*'Hokhmah* is on the active or male side; alternatively, it may be assumed that both *Binah* and *'Hokhmah* were emanated at the same instant and that each exists within the other. The letter of *Kether* is י (*Yod*), and the letter of *Binah* is ה (*Heh*); together they form *YaH*, the feminine Name (compare previous page 175). The third letter, belonging to *'Hokhmah*, is ו (*Vav*), making together יהו (*YHV*) of יהוה (*YHVH*), the Tetragrammaton, which contains the complete symbols of its power. The final ה (*Heh*) of this Ineffable Name is always applied to the six lower Sephiroth and the very last one—together forming the remaining seven Sephiroth. This name finds its resting place in the last Sephirah, *Malkhuth* (Kingdom), the 10th Sephirah, which is the harmony of all the Sephiroth. 

The first three Sephiroth, as we mentioned above, are called the Holy Upper Sephiroth. Together they form a Triad that is a Unity. In the Qabbalah, this is considered the most sacred of all the Sephiroth, as it includes all the others. It is termed the Upper Holy Triad, as well as *Olam ha-Moos'kal* <note>the Intellectual World or Condition</note>.

The *Zohar* says: "The *At-teek-ah Qadosha* <note>the Holy Ancient One</note>—May Its Name be Blessed!—exists with Three Heads, which together form only One Head, and that Head is Itself, which is the most elevated among the highest things. And because the *At-teek-ah Qadosha*—May Its Name be Blessed!—is represented by the Three, all the other Lights (Sephiroth) which enlighten us by their rays are equally comprised in the number Three" (*Zohar*, *Idrah Zootah* <note>Lesser Assembly</note>, iii, 288b). Another statement is: "There are Three Heads engraved one within the other, and one above the other. In this number, first count the mysterious Wisdom—that concealed Wisdom which is never seen without a veil. This Mysterious Wisdom is the supreme principle of all other Wisdom. Above that first Head is the Ancient One—May Its Name be Sanctified!—which is the most mysterious among the mysteries. Finally comes the Head which dominates all others; a Head which is not a Head. What it contains none know nor can know, because it escapes our knowledge and our ignorance. It is for that reason that the Ancient One—whose Name be Blessed!—is called *Ayin* <note>the No-Thing</note>." 

"Each point of matter has three directions: Length, Breadth, and Depth. There does not exist anything below whose root—that is, its perfect prototype—is not above. Therefore, it is necessary that these three have a spiritual root in the first point above. They are therefore called, in their spiritual nature in the primitive Upper Point: *Kether*, *'Hokhmah*, and *Binah*" (*Sepher Shepathal*, folio 49, column 3).

# Hertochdom Milanen.

Dit Hertochdom wordt voor het befte Hertochdom der geheelder Chriftenheyt gheacht, ghelijck Vlaenderen het befte Graeffchap; ghelijck wij te dyer plaetfen ghefeyt hebben. Het is een feer coftelyck ende vruchtbaer landt (gelijck om fegghen geheel Lombardyen is, daert een deel af is), de principael ftadt daer in is Milanen, daer 't hertochdom finen naem na heeft. Defe ftadt is feer vermaert ende beker-it geworden deur de oorlogen in onfen tijden, dier tuffchen den Keyfer Carolus de vijfde, en Francifcus de eerfte van dyen naeme Coninck van Vranckrijck om gevoert fijn geweeft; ende oock deur haer Cafteel datter aen leet, dwelck onder alle fterckten der Chriftenheyt eenē grootē naem heeft. Men telt defe ftadt voor eene vande grootfte fteden van Europa: ende fal oock wel metter tijt de ftercfte beeten, waren de mueren ende bolwercken rontsomme volmaect, daer wij An. 1559. aen fagen wercken. Hoewel dat defe ftadt foo groot is ende naer advenant vol volcks, foo is te verwonderen datter de lijfneeringe foo goeden coop is; maer dat maeckt het vruchtbaer aertrijck daerfe in ghelegen is, ende foo veel wateren ende beken daerfe rontsom van wt het gheberchte en de groote Riviere Po mede gedient wordt; waer deur alle dingen die den menfche nootelyck fijn, oft tot vermaeck ende luft begheert worden, overvloedelyck ende goeden coop, ghebracht worden. Soo groote menichte van alderleye Cunften en hantwercken fijn hier, dattet nauwelyck te gelooven en is; alfoo dat in Italien een fpreecwoort is, Wie Italien beteren wilde, moefte Milanen verderven; te weten, dat hun alfoo de Cunftenaren ende wercklieden hier wt verjaecht fijnde, deur geheel Italien ftroyen ende verbreyden fouden. Seer veel coftelycke ende treffelycke edificien ende ghebouwen fijnder, onder de welcke de principaelste is de opperfte Kercke den Dom gheheeten, waer aen de Cunfte met de Coftelyckheyt fchijnen om prijs te vechten. Ick hebbe fomtijts ghefeyt dattet my dochte een Bagge te fyne, om datfe van onder tot boven met Marmoren beelden, ende alderley ander cieraet ende gefnedenwerck foo overvloedelyck van buyten becleet is, datfe fchijnt niet van Steenbouders, maer van Siluerfmeden gemaect te fyne. De andere Kercken ende Heeren-huyfen fouden hier te lanck fijn te befchryven. Maer die een Burgers oft priuaet perfoons huys wil fien, die gae te Milanen ende vraghe nae het huys dat Tomas de Marini Genewois daer heeft laten maken, (ick dencke dattet nu voldaen is) ende dat van buyten en van binnen wel deur fien hebbende, mach hy hem wel voor laten ftaen, algaet hy verde dat hi nerghens gheen coftelycker oft mogelyck diefghelycx fien en fal. Dit meyne ick dat met my fegghen fullen, alle die haer fulcx verftaende, landen ende Steden befocht hebben. Andere fteden onder dit Hertochdom gheleghen, fijn Pauia feer vermaert deur de hooghe fchole dyer is, ende den flach die fynen onfterffelycken naem van haer heeft, ende by haer ghefchiede An. 1525. daer in Francifcus de Coninck van Vranckrijck ghevangen werdt; daer nae Crema, Lodi certijts Laus Pompeia gheheeten, Como van ghelegentheyt feer playfant, ghelijck wij op haer plaetfe fegghen fullen, ende andere.

# Duchy of Milan.

This Duchy is considered the best Duchy of all Christendom, just as Flanders is the best County; as we have said in those places. It is a very precious and fertile land (as is indeed the whole of Lombardy, of which it is a part); the principal city therein is Milan, from which the Duchy has its name. This city is very famous and has become well-known through the wars in our times, which were waged between the Emperor Charles the Fifth and Francis the First of that name, King of France; and also through its Castle that lies there, which has a great name among all the fortresses of Christendom. One counts this city as one of the largest cities of Europe: and it will also likely in time be the strongest, were the walls and bastions round about completed, on which we saw work being done in the year 1559. Although this city is so large and proportionally full of people, it is still to be wondered at that food is so cheap there; but that is caused by the fertile soil in which it is situated, and so many waters and streams with which it is surrounded and served from the mountains and the great river Po; through which all things that are necessary for man, or desired for pleasure and delight, are brought in abundantly and at a good price. So great a multitude of all kinds of arts and crafts are here, that it is hardly to be believed; so that there is a proverb in Italy: "He who would improve Italy, must destroy Milan"; meaning that the artists and workmen, being chased out of here, would scatter and spread through all of Italy. There are very many precious and excellent edifices and buildings, among which the most principal is the supreme church, called the <term>Dom</term> <gloss>Cathedral</gloss>, where art and costliness seem to fight for the prize. I have sometimes said that it seemed to me to be a trinket, because it is so abundantly covered from bottom to top with marble statues and all kinds of other ornament and carved work on the outside, that it seems to be made not by stonemasons, but by silversmiths. The other churches and noble houses would be too long to describe here. But he who wants to see a citizen's or private person's house, let him go to Milan and ask for the house that Tomas de Marini, a Genoese, has had made there (I think it is now finished), and having seen it well through from outside and inside, he may well boast to himself, even if he travels far, that he will nowhere see anything more precious or possibly like it. This I think all who have visited lands and cities with such understanding will say with me. Other cities situated under this Duchy are Pavia, very famous through the university that is there, and the battle that has its immortal name from it, and happened near it in the year 1525, where Francis, the King of France, was captured; thereafter Crema, Lodi, formerly called <term>Laus Pompeia</term> <gloss>the Roman name for Lodi</gloss>, Como, very pleasant in its situation, as we shall say in its place, and others.

<margin>2</margin>is attributed to cattle: but it is wrong for the good to be mixed with evils, and it is not even common to many. And that pleasure is not the most powerful thing: but the good is the most powerful. And that it is an impediment to doing honorable things: for how can that which prevents one from doing honorable things be good? Therefore, we must first address the first point, regarding its origin, and dispel the argument that it is by no means true. Thus, in the first place, not every pleasure is a process of generation. For the pleasure that arises from looking is not a process of generation; nor is that 
<margin>10</margin>which arises from hearing and smelling. For they are not produced from a deficiency, as is the case in others, such as from eating or drinking. For these occur from a deficiency and a surplus, either by satisfying a deficiency or by removing a surplus: therefore, they seem to be processes of generation. But deficiency and surplus are a sickness: therefore, there is a sickness where there is a process of generation of pleasure. Yet, in looking, hearing, and smelling, it is not the case that sickness precedes it; for no one who takes pleasure in looking or smelling has been in distress beforehand. Likewise in thought: for there can be pleasure for the one contemplating some matter without a preceding distress; and consequently, there will be some pleasure which is not a process of generation. But if pleasure, 
<margin>20</margin>as their argument dictates, is not good because it is a process of generation, and there is some pleasure which is not a process of generation, then pleasure would surely be good. Yet pleasure is not a process of generation in its entirety: for the pleasures from eating and drinking cannot be called processes of generation. But those who claim that these pleasures are processes of generation hallucinate; they think, indeed, that since pleasure is generated when objects are brought forward (or while taking food), it is for this reason a process of generation. But it is not: for since there is a certain part of the soul by which we are delighted as soon as the things we needed are brought forward, that part of the soul is delighted insofar as it is exercised and moved. Yet the motion itself and the exercise is pleasure. Which, 
<margin>30</margin>when that part of the soul is exercised with the objects brought forward, they think is a process of generation because of its action, because the bringing forward of things is certain, but the part of the soul is uncertain, just as if one were to opine that a human being is the body, because it falls under the senses, and not the soul: but it is the soul. Likewise, it is also in this case. For there is a certain part of the soul by which we are delighted, which is exercised as soon as the objects are brought forward: therefore, no pleasure is a process of generation. But they say there is also a conversion into nature, which falls under the senses. For when they are not converting themselves into nature, there is no pleasure, since by converting, 
<margin>1205</margin>a saturation is made from the deficiency of nature. But, as we have said, it is possible for enjoyment to occur without any deficiency, since a deficiency is a sickness, but we say that someone can be delighted without sickness; and consequently, pleasure would not be the conversion of a deficiency. For there is nothing unworthy in such pleasures. Consequently, if pleasure is judged to be good because it is a process of generation, and no pleasure is a process of generation, then pleasure would indeed be good. Furthermore, they say that not every pleasure is good, which anyone might detect in this way: for because the good is said to be in all 
<margin>10</margin>predicaments, namely in essence, in relation to something, in quantity, in time, and in everything in all things, it is also manifest that some pleasure accompanies everything. Therefore, because the good is in all predicaments, pleasure also would be good. And consequently, since in these there are things good in themselves, pleasure would also be a good in itself. Yet pleasure is a pleasure of goods: therefore, every pleasure would be good. At the same time, it is certain from this that pleasures also differ in species among themselves, since the predicaments in which pleasure exists also differ. For it is not as it is in the sciences, 
<margin>20</margin>such as grammar or any other. If Lamprus possesses grammar, and this grammarian is affected by this grammar in the same way as any other person possessing grammar, there are certainly not two different grammars, the one in Lamprus and the one in Ileus. But it is not so in pleasure: for the pleasure that comes from drunkenness and that from sexual intercourse do not affect one in the same way; for which reason, pleasures will seem to be distinguished among themselves by species. Furthermore, because there are also evil pleasures, for this reason too, pleasure seemed not to be good. But that judgment is by no means proper to pleasure, but to nature and science. For there is also 
<margin>30</margin>an evil nature, such as that of worms, wasps, and utterly vile animals; yet it is not because of this that nature is evil. In the same way, there are also evil sciences, such as sedentary ones; yet it is not because of this that science is evil, but rather good in its genus, both science and nature. For just as a sculptor is not to be judged as to what sort of person he is from what he committed through error and did badly, but rather from what he did well, so neither is science 

<column-break/>

nor nature nor anything else to be judged as to what it is from its evils, but from its good qualities. Therefore, pleasure also is good in its genus. That indeed 
<margin>5</margin>there are also evil pleasures does not escape us. For there are also diverse natures of animals, good and bad, just as those of a human are good, but those of a wolf or any other wild beast are bad. Similarly, the nature of a horse is different from that of a human, and that of an ass and a dog. But pleasure is a conversion from that which is against nature, into the nature of each one; consequently, this also would be most sweet. Yet an evil nature has an evil pleasure. For what is for a horse is not for a human, and not even for others. But since there are diverse natures, there are also diverse pleasures. For pleasure is a conversion; and they say conversion, or restoration, restores to nature. Consequently, an evil nature has an evil conversion, just as a good one has a good one. Furthermore, those who contend that pleasure is not good are affected in the way that those are who are unfamiliar with nectar and think the gods drink wine, and that nothing is sweeter than that: they fall into this out of ignorance. A similar thing happens to those who assert that all pleasures are processes of generation, and by no means good. For because they ignore other pleasures besides 
<margin>20</margin>those of the body, they consider them to be processes of generation and not good: they do not think that pleasure in general is good. Since, therefore, there is both a pleasure of restoring nature and one of a nature already restored (the former are, of course, replenishments after a defect, but the latter are those which are perceived by the eyes and ears, and similar things), the functions of a nature that has been restored and obtains its own state, so to speak, seem to be better. For pleasures, spoken of in either way, are actions. Therefore, there is no doubt that pleasures from sight, hearing, and intelligence are by far the best, since those that fall under the body are produced from replenishment. Again, it was said that it is not even good, since that which is in everything and common to all is not good. That is certainly more proper to 
<margin>30</margin>the lover of honor and the desire for honor, for only the lover of honor wishes to have it and to surpass others in it. Should pleasure, therefore, if it must be good in itself, be of this kind, or not? Yet it is also in the opposite way. For it might seem to be good because all things seek it: for it is innate in all to seek the good. And consequently, if all things seek pleasure, pleasure would be good in its genus. Again, they denied that pleasure is good because it is an impediment, asserting that it is an impediment; which they do not seem to consider rightly. For it is not an impediment to the completion of matters, if there is any other impediment, as the pleasure of drunkenness might inhibit one from acting. Furthermore, in that way, science would also be an impediment to science: for it is not possible for you to exercise both at the same time. But why is science not good if pleasure is excited from science? And whether it is an impediment or not? Furthermore, it will act much more: for pleasure, once aroused, impels one to act more, because by doing what is right 
<margin>10</margin>it does what is from virtue, and does it sweetly. Will it not exercise much more those things that pertain to action? And if one acts while delighted, one will be good: but if one pursues honorable things while distressed, one is not good. For there is distress in those things that are from necessity. Consequently, if someone is affected by pain while pursuing honorable things, one performs them under compulsion: but one who is compelled to act from necessity is not good. Furthermore, no one can act in accordance with virtue without being affected by some pleasure or distress: for there is no middle ground. Why? Namely 
<margin>20</margin>because virtue is in an affection, and an affection is in distress and pleasure; nor is anything placed in the middle. There is no doubt, therefore, that virtue is with distress or pleasure. If anyone, therefore, pursues honorable things while sad, he is not good. Consequently, virtue would not be with distress: therefore with pleasure. It is, therefore, so far from being an impediment that it even exhorts one to act. And in total, it does not happen to be without pleasure, because it is produced by it itself. Another argument was that no science produces pleasure. That is not true either. For the builders of banquets and garlands, as well as perfumers, are producers of pleasure. Furthermore, for other sciences, pleasure is not the end, but it is with pleasure and not without pleasure. ## Rushes.

**A**lthough there are many kindes of Rushes, yet I shall onely here insist upon those which are best known, and most Medicinal, as the Bulrushes, and other of the soft and smooth kindes ; which grow so commonly in almost every place of this Land, and are so generally noted, that I suppose it needlesse to trouble you with any Description of them: Briefly then take the Vertues of them as followeth.

<margin>*Government and Vertues.*</margin>
The Seeds of these soft Rushes, saith *Dioscorides* and *Galen*, toasted (saith *Pliny*) being drunk in Wine and Water, stayeth the Lask and Womens Courses, when they come down too abundantly : but it causeth Headach : It provoketh sleep likewise, but must be given with caution, lest the party that takes it wake not untill the Resurrection : *Pliny* saith, The Root boyled in water to the consumption of one third, helpeth the Cough.

Thus you see that Conveniences have their Inconveniencies, and Vertue is seldome unaccompanied with some Vices. What I have writen concerning Rushes is to satisfie my Country-mens Question, *Are our Rushes good for nothing?* Yes, and as good let alone as taken ; There are Remedies enough without them for any Disease, and therefore as the Proverb is I care not a Rush for them, or rather they wil do you as much good as if one had given you a Rush.

## Rye.

**T**his is so well known in all the Countries of this Land, and especially to the Country People who feed much thereon, that if I should describe it, they would presently say, I might well have spared that Labour :

<margin>*Its Vertues follow. Impostums Boyls & Swellings, pains of the Head, Chops of the Hands or Feet.*</margin>
*Government and Vertues.*] Rye is more digesting then Wheat ; The Bread and the Leaven thereof ripeneth and breaketh Impostumes, Boyls, and other Swellings : The Meal of Rye put between a double cloth, and moistened with a little Vinegar, and heated in a Pewter dish, set over a Chafingdish of coals; and bound fast to the head while it is hot, both much ease the continual pains of the Head. *Mathiolus* saith, That the Ashes of Rye straw put into Water, and suffered therein a day and a night, and the Chops of the Hands or Feet washed therewith, doth heal them.

...the inconceivable knowledge of becoming, the inconceivable knowledge of the explanation of becoming, the inconceivable knowledge of the defiled becoming, and the inconceivable knowledge of the purified becoming; these are the four. Youth, these are the four knowledges of entities of the Bodhisattvas; what are the four? The inconceivable knowledge of entities of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of entities of the explanation of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of entities of the defiled, and the inconceivable knowledge of entities of the purified; these are the four. Youth, these are the four knowledges of persons of the Bodhisattvas; what are the four? The inconceivable knowledge of persons of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of persons of the explanation of compositional factors, the inconceivable knowledge of persons of the defiled, and the inconceivable knowledge of persons of the purified; these are the four. Youth, these are the four knowledges of objects of the Bodhisattvas; they are inconceivable, and the four teachings that are inconceivable; they are not to be taught as ultimate states.

Whatever desire there is for the knowledge of phenomena, that is called the perfect knowledge of the individual definitions of words. This means teaching, explaining, applying, demonstrating, elevating, analyzing, and correctly differentiating phenomena knowledge; it is making it clear, having unobstructed words, having words that are not cast away, not stammering, not being confused, and having words without hesitation; this, Youth, is called the perfect knowledge of individual oratorical power. Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

As many as are the wisdoms of the Buddhas,
So many are the designations of form.
As many as are the designations of form,
So many are the names spoken of form.
As many as are the spoken names of form,
So many are the names of morality.
As many as are the names of morality,
So many are the names of the Buddhas.
As many as are the names of the Buddhas,
So many are the names of sentient beings.
The names of a single sentient being,
I have explained as being that many.
Names and speech are infinite;
Those which I have previously explained,
The names of morality and the names of the Buddhas,
The names of sentient beings are equivalent to them.
As many as are the faults of the conditioned,
So many are the praises of nirvana.
